1.pericope_label: Praise ye the name of the Lord: the summons to his servants and the choosing of Jacob

schools.summary: Augustine presses the fact of standing within rather than without, and argues that servants who might yet gain the privilege of sons owe praise all the more.

Calvin holds that the people and not the Levites only are addressed, while allowing the priests the lead, and prefers the reading that makes the singing rather than the name the pleasant thing; Gill takes the chosen Jacob for the whole church of Jews and Gentiles rather than for the person or the nation.

Henry includes both priests and worshippers, makes the work its own wages since praising God is a heaven upon earth, and holds the seed of Jacob most ungrateful if they do not praise; Spurgeon counts the threefold call and turns the servants into court-musicians.

Clarke connects the psalm with the one before it and with an earlier psalm and a prophet, infers a date after the captivity and a possible use at the dedication of the second temple, and numbers the reasons for praise as they come.

Ellicott takes the address as priestly and calls the wider application possible but unproved, prefers play to sing, and glosses the covenant-name for Israel; Keil and Delitzsch describe the psalm as mosaic work assembled from the Law, the Prophets and the Psalms.

debates: Who is summoned to praise? Ellicott takes the priestly class to be addressed as in the psalm before and calls the wider application possible but not proved; Calvin argues that the people generally are addressed since the reasons apply to all and the night watching is not mentioned, while still allowing the priests the lead and finding the people implied in the plural courts; Henry includes priests, Levites and worshippers together.

What is it that is pleasant? Calvin allows both that the name is sweet and that singing praise is sweet, and prefers the latter because the word properly signifies what is seemly or beautiful; Ellicott agrees it is the singing of the hallelujah while noting that others make the name the subject; Henry answers that the work is its own wages; Clarke counts it simply as the second reason for praise.
outliers: Keil and Delitzsch describe the psalm as mosaic work, borrowing from a Latin poet the image of words fitted together like little tesserae, and observe that this one draws its pieces from the Law, the Prophets and the Psalms alike.
Ellicott notes that the Prayer Book rendering of this verse suggested to Crashaw the hymn beginning Come lovely name.
themes: praise urged upon those nearest the house
a psalm assembled out of older psalms
the pleasure of praising as its own reward
a people chosen as a peculiar treasure
ingratitude as the only alternative

5.pericope_label: For I know that the Lord is great: his pleasure done in heaven and earth, and the vapours from the ends of the earth

schools.summary: Henry makes greatness the matter of awful praise as goodness was of cheerful, grounds the assertion in experience and a holy defiance of pretenders, holds that God does what he pleases because he pleases and gives no account, and finds fire and water reconciled in the lightnings that bring rain.

Gill distributes the greatness through the persons of the Godhead with a different ground of knowledge for each, contrasts divine sovereignty with the limits of despotic princes, and reports three older readings of the vapours including a mystical one.

Clarke numbers the reasons for praise as they come, reverses the order of pleasure and rightness in the divine will, and prefers clouds to vapours on the authority of a traveller account of the autumnal rains; Wesley extends the range to the invisible depths of earth and water.

Ellicott refers the vapours to the mist of the creation story and defends the identification against the difference of term, explains the lightnings as bringing rain after the eastern notion, and compares the treasuries of the wind with the classical caves of the winds; Keil and Delitzsch guard the phrase from meaning that lightnings are turned into rain.

debates: What are the vapours that ascend? Gill reports an older reading that takes them for the mist which went up out of the earth, another that takes them for clouds named from their elevation, and a father who expounds the clouds of the apostles and prophets; Ellicott judges the mist of the creation story undoubtedly right and answers the objection that a different term is used there; Clarke prefers clouds on the strength of a traveller account of the autumnal rains, where a squall of wind and clouds of dust forerun the first rain.

Why does God do whatsoever he pleases? Henry answers that he does what he pleases because he pleases and gives not an account of any of his matters; Clarke reverses it, holding that all he has done is right and therefore pleasing in his sight; Gill approaches by contrast, that even the most arbitrary princes cannot do everything they please while he can and does.
outliers: Gill reports a father who expounds the clouds mystically of the apostles and prophets, raised from a low and mean estate to carry good doctrine about the world.
Henry finds in the lightnings made for rain a reconciliation of fire and water by divine omnipotence, the two coming together without the water quenching the fire or the fire licking up the water.
themes: greatness as the matter of awful praise
a will that gives no account of itself
sovereignty reaching the invisible depths
the origin of cloud, rain and wind
wind kept in treasuries

8.pericope_label: Who smote the firstborn of Egypt: the plagues, the conquest, and the enduring name

schools.summary: Gill expounds the plagues and the conquest typically, with the passover blood an emblem and the conqueror and the lawgiver both types, yet steps back at one verse to prefer an older Jewish reading of the kings, and offers two constructions of the judging of his people.

Clarke declines to comment on the smiting of the firstborn and refers the reader to the parallel passages; Wesley divides the closing verse between a cause pleaded in due time and a severe sentence recalled.

Ellicott traces the abrupt turn from nature to history to the next psalm and identifies two verses as taken from the law, and renders the judging as seeing the people righted; Keil and Delitzsch show the language of the conquest to be Deuteronomic throughout, correct the nations from many to great, and make the enduring name the hinge of the psalm.

debates: Are the nations many or great? Keil and Delitzsch insist on great rather than many, since the parallel word is meant not of a powerful number but of powerful might, while Gill takes the other reading and counts the seven nations by name with their kings at thirty-one.

What is meant by the Lord judging his people? Gill offers two constructions, that he rules, protects and avenges them, or that he chastises them in a fatherly way so that they may not be condemned with the world; Ellicott compresses it into seeing them righted; Wesley makes it the pleading of their cause in due time, with the repenting a recall of the sentence passed for their sins.
outliers: Gill steps back from his own typological expansion at the mention of the great nations, reporting that an older Jewish commentator refers the words to the kings of Midian or to those next named, and judging that reading best.
Ellicott traces the abrupt change from the miracles of nature to the marvels of history to imitation, saying it is apparently copied from the psalm that follows this one.
themes: plagues remembered as deliverance
a conquest recounted in borrowed words
a name outlasting the generations
judgment as vindication or as chastening
the living God set against idols

15.pericope_label: The idols of the heathen are silver and gold: the senseless gods and their senseless makers

schools.summary: Henry argues from the making that the idols can return no power to their makers, calls the giving of eyes and nostrils to them a jest, and draws the moral that senseless worship makes senseless worshippers; Spurgeon calls the worship of metallic manufactures insanity, thinks idols fitter for children to play with than for men to adore, and turns the comparison against lukewarm believers.

Gill works from the material of the idols to the God who owns the metals, and records that the closing verse may be read either as a statement that the makers are as senseless as their work or as a wish that they may become so.
Clarke declines to expound the passage since it repeats an earlier psalm almost word for word, and notes a manuscript that restores the two verses this psalm omits.

Keil and Delitzsch show the passage following the earlier psalm with abridgments and find in the surviving particle and in the denial of breath the traces of what was dropped, and render the clause as denying any being of breath at all.

debates: What has been abridged in this passage, and does it matter? Clarke declines to comment because the verses repeat an earlier psalm almost word for word, and reports one manuscript that adds the omitted verses back in this place; Keil and Delitzsch describe the same abridgment from within, finding in the particle used here a trace of the organ of smell mentioned there and in the denial of breath a trace of the denial of smelling; Henry notes that the earlier psalm draws from the same argument the duty of trusting where this one draws the duty of blessing.

Is the closing verse a statement or a wish? Gill records that the words may be read either as saying that those who make idols are as blind and senseless as their work, or, with some versions and interpreters, as a prayer that they may become so; Henry and Spurgeon take the plain statement, Henry extending it from the makers to those who trust in them.
outliers: Clarke reports a manuscript which restores into this psalm the two verses that the parallel passage contains and this one leaves out.
Spurgeon judges idols fitter to be played with like dolls by babes than to be adored by grown men, and holds that hands are better used in breaking such objects than in making them.
themes: gods made of metal by hand
organs of sense without sense
worship shaping the worshipper
a description or an imprecation
a passage repeated from another psalm

19.pericope_label: Bless the Lord, O house of Israel: the fourfold summons and the blessing out of Zion

schools.summary: Spurgeon reads the four groups as rings that narrow to the house of Aaron and widen again through Levi to all who fear the Lord, so that adoration may spread from man to man until the whole lump is leavened.

Gill distinguishes the two priestly houses by office and reports a Jewish reading that confines the Levites to the singers, and takes the closing formula as pointing both to the persons who bless and to the place, adding that even doorkeepers have reason to bless God for a place there.
Clarke declines to comment on the summons and refers the reader to the parallel psalm, and reads the closing verse as the praise of a people whose temple and city have been restored.

Ellicott makes the blessing out of Zion the reciprocal of a blessing given from Zion and notes the emphasis added by naming the city as well as the hill; Keil and Delitzsch count the call as fourfold where earlier psalms have three, and treat Zion as the place from which the attestation of God by the mouth of men is to spread.

debates: How is the closing summons arranged? Keil and Delitzsch count it as fourfold where two earlier psalms have a threefold call, the house of the Levites being added here, and note that a blessing merely wished in the short psalm before has become an ascription of praise; Spurgeon reads the groups as rings narrowing to the house of Aaron and widening again until adoration spreads through the whole lump of humanity; Gill separates the houses by office and reports a reading that confines the Levites to the temple singers.

What is meant by blessing the Lord out of Zion? Ellicott makes it the answer to a blessing given from Zion, the place where the relation between God and his people is best realised; Keil and Delitzsch make Zion the place from which the attestation of God by human mouths is to be spread abroad, and say history has realized it; Gill reports an older view that the words are the formula of blessing itself; Clarke reads them of a restored temple and city.
outliers: Spurgeon turns the four groups into narrowing and widening rings, ending with the hope that reverence will spread from man to man until the whole lump of humanity is leavened.
Gill observes that even doorkeepers in the house of the Lord have reason to bless his name for a place there.
themes: a summons widened to include the Levites
office as a reason for leading praise
fear of God as the last qualification
blessing given and returned at one place
a city restored and inhabited
